# Optimal Control
Mathematical models of cancer describe how tumor populations evolve over time and how they interact with the immune system, treatment, and their surrounding environment. While these models can provide insight into tumor dynamics and treatment response, they often assume that treatment is prescribed according to a fixed schedule.

Optimal control theory extends this framework by treating therapy as a time-dependent decision variable. Rather than simply predicting tumor evolution under a prescribed treatment, we seek a treatment strategy that optimizes a specified therapeutic objective.

In cancer modeling, this objective typically involves balancing tumor reduction against treatment-related toxicity, drug consumption, or damage to healthy tissue. The resulting mathematical problem combines a system of differential equations describing tumor dynamics with an objective functional measuring the
performance of a treatment strategy.

Optimal control has been applied to several cancer treatment problems, including chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and combination therapy. Examples include studies of competing chemotherapy strategies, immune mediated tumor dynamics, and treatment optimization in the presence of drug resistance.

This chapter introduces the mathematical foundations of optimal control for ordinary differential equation (ODE) models of cancer. We begin with the general formulation of an optimal control problem, followed by Pontryagin’s Maximum Principle and the derivation of the associated optimality system. A Gompertzian
tumor-growth model is then used to illustrate the derivation and numerical solution of an optimal treatment strategy using the forward–backward sweep method.
